hook.line: Tomás asks everyone about the young man in Rosa's photo. Nobody knows anything, or nobody will say. Spanish has a handful of small words for that kind of answer, and it says *no* twice.

examples.es: Nadie habla del joven de la foto.
examples.en: Nobody talks about the young man in the photo.

examples.es: No tengo ninguna foto de mi abuelo.
examples.en: I don't have a single photo of my grandfather.

examples.es:
¿Conoces a alguien en Bogotá?
No, a nadie.
examples.en:
Do you know anyone in Bogotá?
No, nobody.

rule:
Five words do the saying-no work:

*nada*: nothing, anything
*nadie*: nobody, anybody
*nunca*: never
*tampoco*: not either, neither
*ningún*, *ninguna*: not one, no

The surprise: Spanish doubles up. If one of these words comes after the verb, *no* still goes in front: *No sé nada*, literally I don't know nothing. That isn't sloppy; it's the only right way.

If the word comes first, drop the *no*: *Nadie sabe*. *Nunca tomo cerveza* and *No tomo cerveza nunca* mean the same.

*Ningún* goes before a masculine word, *ninguna* before a feminine one, and both stay singular: *ningún problema*, *ninguna foto*.

*Tampoco* is the negative *también*: when someone says something negative that's true for you too, say *Yo tampoco*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this double negation. Standard English forbids it; Spanish requires it.

readAndPick.es:

A mí tampoco.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *nada* or *nadie*: No hay ___ en el café. (There's nobody in the café.) Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.answer: No hay nadie en el café.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *nada* or *nadie*: Tomás no sabe ___. (Tomás doesn't know anything.) Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.why: Anything, a thing, is *nada*, with *no* before the verb as well.

yourTurn.prompt: Someone says *No tengo hambre.* You're not hungry either. Choose *también* or *tampoco*: Yo ___.

yourTurn.why: *Nunca* before the verb works alone; after it, add *no*.

yourTurn.prompt: I don't have a single photo of my grandfather. (Use *ninguna*.)
yourTurn.answer: No tengo ninguna foto de mi abuelo.
yourTurn.why: *Foto* is feminine, so *ninguna*, and it stays singular.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative with *nunca*: *Hernando siempre habla de su esposa.*
yourTurn.answer: Hernando nunca habla de su esposa.
accept: Hernando no habla nunca de su esposa.
yourTurn.why: *Nunca* takes the place of *siempre*; before the verb, no extra *no*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *Conozco a alguien en Bogotá.*
yourTurn.answer: No conozco a nadie en Bogotá.
yourTurn.why: *Alguien* flips to *nadie*, and *no* goes before the verb.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After the verb, *nada* needs a *no* in front too: two negatives, one meaning.
When *nadie* comes first, it does the job alone.
*Ningún* stays singular: not a single problem.
Agreeing with a negative takes *tampoco*; *también* is for positive ones.

personal: Write three true sentences: something you never do (*nunca*), something nobody in your family does (*nadie*), and something you don't know anything about (*no sé nada de…*).
